name: Whitening strips

lead: Whitening strips are thin, flexible plastic films coated with a peroxide gel, typically hydrogen peroxide at roughly 6 to 14 percent, that are pressed onto the front teeth for a set time each day over one to several weeks. They are sold over the counter and are the most widely used consumer route to lighter teeth.

In appearance terms they target extrinsic and mild intrinsic discoloration from coffee, tea, wine and age, and are generally regarded as one of the lower-cost and better-supported cosmetic options for the smile. Results fade gradually, and many users repeat short touch-up courses.

paras: Hydrogen peroxide diffuses through enamel and breaks down into reactive oxygen species that cleave the large pigmented molecules lodged in the tooth, converting them into smaller, less colored fragments. The strip holds the gel against the tooth surface so the peroxide stays in contact long enough to act.

The main side effects are transient tooth sensitivity and gum irritation, usually mild and resolving after stopping. Strips cover mostly the front teeth and fit unevenly on crowded or irregular teeth, so coverage can be patchy. The Cochrane review of home bleaching rated much of the evidence as low certainty, while reporting that peroxide whitening itself is consistently shown to lighten teeth. Dental guidance generally advises seeking dental advice before overuse, or before whitening over untreated decay or exposed roots.
